title: Feijoada
subtitle: Brazilian black bean stew with pork
excerpt: A slow-cooked stew of black beans with multiple cuts of pork and beef, scented with orange and bay. This is Brazil's national dish -- a rich, hearty weekend meal that serves a crowd.
sourceNotes: Feijoada is the national dish of Brazil. It has roots in the African slave trade, when enslaved workers made nourishing stews from less desirable cuts of pork. It is now eaten at family gatherings across the country.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions. Reheat slowly on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Feijoada tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and refrigerate.

content.text: Soak the dried black beans overnight -- this is not optional. Drain and cook them fresh with the meat. The cooking liquid becomes the stew broth and needs at least 2 hours to develop properly.

items.prepNote: in one piece or thick-cut slices
smoked sausage if available, cut into chunks

content.text: Drain the soaked beans. Put them in a large pot and cover with cold water by 5cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 45 minutes.
In a separate pan, fry the bacon until the fat renders. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and smoked paprika. Stir for 1 minute.
Add all the meat -- beef, pork shoulder, and sausage -- to the pan with the beans.
Stir in the onion mixture, bay leaves, orange juice, and zest.
Simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours until all the meat is tender and the beans are creamy.
Taste and season generously. Serve with white rice, fresh orange slices, and shredded kale.

items.symptom: Beans are still firm after 2 hours
items.fix: Old dried beans can be stubborn. Continue simmering. A splash of vinegar in the water can sometimes help soften them.

items.cause: Too much water or not simmered down
items.fix: Remove the lid and simmer for an extra 20 minutes to reduce. Remove some beans, mash them, and stir back in to thicken.

items.cause: Pork or beef not cooked long enough
items.fix: Continue simmering. Both cuts need sustained heat. Feijoada should never be rushed.

content.text: Feijoada is Brazil's national dish and one of the country's most important food traditions. It has roots in the West African cooking traditions brought to Brazil during the slave trade, when nourishing stews were made from whatever ingredients were available. Over centuries it became a dish for celebration and community. Today it is eaten at family gatherings, restaurants, and bars across Brazil every weekend.
